reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India national programmes
clinicalPearls: A protozoal infection of the small intestine caused by Giardia, acquired by faecal-oral spread of cysts through contaminated water or food, or person to person
Highly endemic in India, contributing to childhood diarrhoea, malabsorption and faltering growth
Typical illness is prolonged, with foul-smelling greasy diarrhoea, bloating, flatulence, abdominal cramps and weight loss rather than blood or fever
Many infections are asymptomatic, and cyst passage can continue in the absence of symptoms, sustaining transmission
Chronic infection can cause fat and lactose malabsorption and, in children, nutritional deficiencies and stunting
Diagnosis traditionally relies on detecting cysts or trophozoites on repeated stool examination, with stool antigen and PCR tests being more sensitive
Because cyst excretion is intermittent, a single negative stool sample does not exclude infection
Treatment is with antiprotozoal agents; attention to safe water and hygiene prevents reinfection and outbreaks
reference.pathophysiology: Ingested Giardia cysts excyst in the small intestine and release trophozoites that attach to the duodenal and jejunal mucosa via a ventral adhesive disc. Colonisation causes villous shortening, disruption of the brush-border enzymes and a mucosal inflammatory response, impairing absorption of fats, carbohydrates and other nutrients. This produces the characteristic malabsorptive, non-inflammatory diarrhoea. Trophozoites encyst as they pass down the gut, and the environmentally hardy cysts are excreted to continue the cycle.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of chronic or malabsorptive diarrhoea (coeliac disease, tropical sprue)
additionalInvestigations: Repeated stool microscopy for cysts and trophozoites
Stool antigen detection (ELISA) or PCR for greater sensitivity
Duodenal aspirate or biopsy in difficult cases
Assessment for malabsorption and nutritional status in chronic disease
Evaluation for immunoglobulin deficiency in recurrent or refractory infection
redFlags: Severe dehydration or significant weight loss, particularly in young children
Malabsorption with nutritional deficiency and growth faltering
Persistent or relapsing infection suggesting underlying immunodeficiency
Failure to respond to standard therapy, prompting reassessment of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Most cases respond well to antiprotozoal therapy with full recovery. Untreated or recurrent infection, especially in children, can cause lasting malabsorption and growth impairment, and reinfection is common where sanitation is poor.
pitfalls: Excluding giardiasis on the basis of a single negative stool sample despite intermittent cyst shedding
Overlooking it as a treatable cause of chronic diarrhoea and malabsorption
Missing underlying immunodeficiency in recurrent or refractory cases
Neglecting water and hygiene measures, leading to reinfection or household spread
management: Treat with a nitroimidazole antiprotozoal such as metronidazole or tinidazole as first-line therapy, with nitazoxanide or albendazole as alternatives
Rehydrate and correct malabsorption and nutritional deficiencies, with temporary lactose avoidance where intolerance develops
Manage refractory infection with extended or combination therapy, checking adherence and excluding reinfection
Reinforce public health measures of safe water, sanitation, hand hygiene, and treatment of symptomatic household contacts
Investigate for immunoglobulin deficiency in recurrent or treatment-refractory disease
Provide nutritional rehabilitation and growth monitoring in affected children
